India has long prioritised energy efficiency to strengthen energy security, improve productivity, and expand access to affordable energy for all. Key initiatives such as the Perform, Achieve and Trade scheme, Building Energy Codes, and the Ujala programme have helped drive progress across sectors.

In 2025, India was among the global leaders in energy efficiency, with more than $4\%$ improvement in primary energy intensity. This aligns with the pace needed to meet global efficiency goals by 2030 and supports India's updated NDC, which targets a $47\%$ reduction in GDP emission intensity by 2035 and $60\%$ non-fossil installed power capacity by 2035. India has already achieved a $37.38\%$ reduction in emission intensity by 2022 and $53.21\%$ non-fossil installed power capacity by March 2026, underscoring the central role of energy efficiency in its clean energy transition.

The Bureau of Energy Efficiency is strengthening the energy efficiency market through innovative financing mechanisms. Its ADEETIE scheme is helping MSMEs adopt efficient technologies through interest subvention and technical support, while also improving project bankability.

Financial de-risking instruments such as energy savings insurance (ESI) have emerged as a promising tool to unlock energy efficiency investment. With a view to de-risk the financing for energy efficiency, BEE has been working with the OECD CEFIM Programme, to develop a roadmap for the design and implementation of ESI in India.

I believe this roadmap will guide stakeholders in designing and implementing an insurance-backed mechanism to support financing, unlock investment, accelerate deployment and support India's broader energy and climate goals.

Editorial

Energy efficiency is a cornerstone of sustainable economic development. In India, it plays a pivotal role in reducing the energy intensity of a rapidly expanding economy, while enhancing affordability and energy security, boosting industrial competitiveness and mitigating emissions. Improving the efficiency of buildings, industry and transport is one of the fastest and most cost-effective ways to reduce energy demand and exposure to external shocks, while enhancing energy sovereignty and economic resilience. Over the past decades, India has made remarkable progress in strengthening its policy framework for energy efficiency. Numerous flagship initiatives led by the Indian Bureau of Energy Efficiency have progressively raised efficiency standards across end-use sectors. Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises, which form the backbone of India's economy, possess untapped potential for achieving energy savings, however barriers prevent higher investment in efficiency improvements.

In this context, the launch of the Energy Savings Insurance (ESI) Implementation Roadmap of India, developed in close collaboration between the Indian Bureau of Energy Efficiency of the Ministry of Power and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, marks an important milestone in unlocking finance and investment for energy efficiency in India. But, of course, it does not stop there. Implementing the roadmap requires collaboration between a multitude of national and international actors in raising awareness, strengthening capacities, piloting and technically supporting the rollout of the ESI scheme.

The OECD, through its Clean Energy Finance and Investment Mobilisation Programme, has worked with the BEE to strengthen India's enabling environment for energy efficiency financing and overcome persisting barriers. This roadmap emerges from a sustained and inclusive collaborative process. The 2022 Clean Energy Finance and Investment Roadmap of India identified Energy Savings Insurance schemes as a key instrument, following extensive cross-ministerial and multi-stakeholder consultations. In the following, the BEE tasked the OECD with developing a dedicated needs assessment and ESI implementation roadmap in India. A jointly organised series of workshops and consultations in 2024-2025 and international lessons from ESI deployment, confirmed the potential of energy savings insurance to substantially reduce the perceived risks of lenders and investors, thereby unlocking private capital for energy efficiency in India's MSMEs and beyond. This roadmap provides a step-by-step guide to tapping into the energy efficiency potential in high priority sectors of the Indian economy through ESI.

We extend our appreciation to the BEE for its leadership and commitment to this initiative. We equally thank the Asian Development Bank, the Ministry of MSMEs, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, the International Institute for Energy Conservation, the many financial institutions, insurers, energy service companies, energy auditors and other experts who contributed to this work. We look forward to continuing our excellent collaboration with the BEE and all partners in supporting the mobilisation of clean energy finance and investment as we move from roadmap to implementation.

Executive summary

India is at a critical juncture where rising energy demand needs to be met in alignment with its ambitious climate objectives and intentions to improve the efficiency of its economy. Increasing India's share of clean energy in total installed capacity and reducing the country's emissions intensity are significant steps towards achieving its sustainable development and climate commitments. As of October 2024, India installed 203 GW of renewable energy and reduced the emission intensity of its GDP by $33\%$ (from 2005-2019), bringing it closer to achieving its 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) targets. As India advances towards its goal of attaining developed nation status by 2047 under its "Viksit Bharat 2047" initiative, it remains committed to provide clean, reliable and affordable energy for all citizens.

India's energy sector is experiencing tremendous growth mirroring the country's booming population and economic development. Over the past decade, India's peak electricity demand has surged by $79\%$ , while total electricity consumption doubled, growing at an annual rate of $5.8\%$ (Bureau of Energy Efficiency, 2024[1]).

India's energy policy reforms of the past twenty years focused on creating the enabling conditions to deliver on the government's ambitions to ensure affordable, secure and sustainable energy services for all Indians. The country's transition towards clean energy is a crucial component of India's overall energy strategy, which requires a holistic approach encompassing advances in technology, policy and investment. Policies promoting a tripling of renewable energy generation capacity and doubling of the rate of energy efficiency (EE) improvement by 2030 play a crucial role in accelerating this transition. Core policies promoting energy efficiency improvements in India include the 2008 National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC), the 2011 National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (NMEEE) including the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme for industries, but also standards and labelling schemes for appliances, Unnat Jyoti by Affordable LEDs for All (UJALA) scheme, the Energy Conversation Building Code, Electric Vehicle Mission and demand side management programmes. In fiscal year 2023-34, these achieved energy savings of approximately 54 million tonnes of oil equivalent, which corresponds to $6\%$ of the nation's total primary energy supply (Bureau of Energy Efficiency, 2024[1]). Over the past twenty years, these have contributed to India's remarkable progress towards higher energy efficiency, with total energy supply per unit of GDP (PPP) decreasing by $36\%$ between 2000 and 2023 (IEA, 2026[2]).

Achieving India's ambitious clean energy and climate goals, however, requires the mobilisation of significant investment in energy efficiency improvements, which has to be supported through an enabling policy framework and appropriate financing and risk mitigation instruments to unlock the necessary capital.
Barriers to energy efficiency financing

Despite its potential, India's energy efficiency market faces several challenges that complicate the acceleration of energy efficiency improvements and scaling up of investments. Information asymmetries, capacity constraints, lack of access to capital and competing investment priorities remain key barriers to scaling the energy efficiency market in India, which are particularly challenging for MSMEs.

Many financiers, investors and end users lack a full understanding of the financial, environmental and operational benefits of energy efficiency projects, which is partly due to the unavailability of long-term performance data for energy efficient appliances and equipment available in the Indian market and leads to higher risk perception. While some energy efficiency measures such as energy management systems can be implemented at no or low costs, energy efficient technologies often require higher upfront investment compared to less efficient alternatives. In a price sensitive market like India with high-risk perception of customers regarding the future performance of efficient technologies and systems, and a short-term investment perspective, this can discourage investment in solutions that deliver significant reductions in operating expenses in the long run. According to the BEE, only around 130 ESCOs are currently empanelled $^{1}$ . While the energy efficiency market in India is estimated to be worth INR 150 000 crore, Energy Service Companies (ESCOs) only tapped about 5% of this market potential (Bureau of Energy Efficiency, 2026 $^{[3]}$ ).

These barriers can be addressed through a range of measures, including by strengthening the regulatory framework and local ESCO market, enhancing capacities for energy efficiency improvements and financing and incentivising investment in energy efficiency. Dedicated financing instruments for energy efficiency projects in different end-use sectors and the deployment of risk mitigation instruments such as guarantee and insurance products can further promote energy efficiency investment.
Aim of the roadmap and its audience

This Energy Savings Insurance (ESI) Implementation Roadmap aims to provide a step-by-step guidance for the design and implementation of an Energy Savings Insurance Scheme in India. It shall inform and guide the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), the Ministry of Power (MOP), the Insurance and Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDA) of India, as well as a range of other key stakeholders, including domestic financial institutions such as banks, non-banking financial institutions and insurance companies, but also insurance associations, ESCOs, energy efficiency technology providers and vendors, industry associations, validation entities, multilateral development banks and international institutions active in India.
What is an Energy Savings Insurance (ESI) scheme?

The Energy Savings Insurance (ESI) model has been designed to mitigate the performance risks of energy efficiency projects, thereby enhancing the creditworthiness of the investors in energy efficient technologies and processes. The ESI scheme is typically implemented as a package of financial and non-financial components, including the energy savings insurance product, a standardised energy performance contract with guaranteed savings, independent technical validation and existing or new financial instruments and incentives that can be linked to energy efficiency projects backed by an ESI. These components work together to reduce perceived risks, build trust in future energy savings among involved stakeholders and mobilise enterprises to invest in energy efficiency solutions.

The model provides a performance guarantee that the contracted energy savings will be achieved through efficiency measures implemented in the project. If the project does not achieve the pledged savings, the provider is obliged to either make necessary improvements or to compensate the client. Should this fail, the guarantor, usually a specialised insurance agency, will financially compensate the client.

The Energy Savings Insurance (ESI) scheme could therefore be instrumental in overcoming persisting market barriers and mobilising investment in energy efficiency in India. International experience in implementing the ESI model, for instance in Latin America, Europe and East Asia, demonstrates its potential to mobilise investment in energy efficiency improvements and achieve the committed savings, as well as its adaptability to specific national contexts and objectives. Key lessons learned from these examples have contributed to shaping the design of the proposed ESI implementation structure in India.
ESI market opportunity, structure and key actors

India's energy efficiency market holds immense potential for scale, driven by rapid industrialisation, urbanisation and increasing energy demand. According to estimates by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), energy efficiency investments across key sectors could reach INR 1 002 329 crores to 1 320 630 crores (USD 121-160 billion) by 2031 (OECD, 2024[6]).

The industrial MSME sector was identified as high-impact opportunity for the implementation of the ESI scheme, thanks to its potential for energy efficiency improvements and for mobilising investment. MSMEs account for 25% of India's energy consumption in the industry sector. Driven by the nation's economic growth and MSME growth, amongst other factors, this consumption is expected to increase by 50% by 2030. Leveraging a unique Indian characteristic, the implementation of an ESI scheme through MSME clusters appears as a promising approach to implement energy efficiency improvements, mobilise financing and achieve better economies of scale and lower transaction costs for participating actors. Here, MSMEs are the beneficiaries of the energy savings insurance, while a standardised energy performance contract is signed between the MSME cluster and an energy service company (ESCO). Following an initial rollout of the ESI scheme in industrial SMEs and at cluster level, the ESI scheme could be expanded to the building sector, and particularly public buildings. The building sector is currently responsible for approximately 35% of India's total energy consumption (Government of India, 2008[4]).

The effective design and implementation of the ESI scheme in India requires close co-ordination and collaboration between a range of stakeholders, capitalising on their unique mandates and strengths. These include public and private sector agencies, financial institutions, validation entities, ESCOs, individual experts and energy auditors, IT and communications experts, regulatory bodies and international institutions. The implementation of an ESI scheme further benefits from technical and financial contributions of development partners, multilateral development banks (MDBs), regional development banks and other development finance institutions (DFIs). The proposed ESI implementation structure explains the roles of the BEE and other public authorities, ESI providers, financial institutions, ESCOs, independent validation entity, MSMEs and the mechanism for fund flow. Linking the ESI scheme with the ADEETIE scheme is a promising approach to enhance the impact of both schemes in promoting energy efficiency improvements in industrial MSMEs.
Implementation plan in India
The proposed implementation plan, or implementation roadmap, provides a step-by-step guide to core actors under the leadership of the BEE for the design and rollout of an effective ESI scheme.
Preparatory phase

As part of the preparatory efforts to introduce an ESI scheme in India, the support from key stakeholders needs to be mobilised to ensure a sustainable anchoring in the Indian market and sufficient uptake of the insurance product. Key domestic stakeholders for the ESI scheme include the General Insurance Council (GIC), participating banks under the ADEETIE scheme and other interested financial institutions, insurance companies (to be identified with support from GIC), the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDAI), ESCOs and energy efficiency technology providers. The implementation of an ESI scheme further benefits from technical and financial contributions of development partners, multilateral development banks (MDBs), regional development banks and other development finance institutions (DFIs).

Preparatory steps for the implementation of an ESI scheme in India include:
• Stakeholder engagement and consultations.
\- Needs assessment and identification of priority sectors for implementation.
• Identification of priority MSME clusters and sub-sector for piloting the ESI scheme.
\- Design of the ESI structure and definition of stakeholder roles.
Implementation phase

The implementation phase of the ESI scheme covers necessary steps to fully operationalise it, pilot it in selected MSME clusters and, based on the learnings derived from this process, roll out the scheme in India.
Key steps to operationalise the ESI scheme include:
• Determining a facilitating entity.
\- Identifying and mandating an independent validation entity and defining monitoring and verification methodologies.
• Developing standardised energy performance contracts and document templates.
• Developing the energy savings insurance product and filing for approval.
\- Designing capacity building and awareness raising campaigns.
Next steps
The BEE will launch the ESI Implementation Roadmap in alignment with the ADEETIE scheme in 2026 to operationalise the ESI scheme.

The BEE will convene a Technical Committee (TC) comprised by main actors for the implementation of the ESI scheme to coordinate implementation activities and ensure alignment with the ADEETIE scheme. The TC should then convene regular meetings under the chairmanship of the DG-BEE.
The design and implementation of ESI pilot projects, and the creation of a pipeline of projects could be coordinated by the TC with guidance from the BEE.

The BEE, supported by the facilitating entity and other partners, should (i) identify capacity building needs of key stakeholders and define targeted training programmes, and (ii) develop standardised templates, contracts and other documents.
Based on the learnings from an initial rollout of both the ESI scheme and the ADEETIE scheme, the BEE could develop a long-term strategy for embedding the ESI scheme in phase II of ADEETIE.

Despite its potential, India's energy efficiency market faces several challenges that complicate the acceleration of energy efficiency improvements and scaling up of investment. Information asymmetries, capacity constraints, lack of access to capital and competing investment priorities remain key barriers to scaling the energy efficiency market in India, and are particularly challenging for MSMEs. Many financiers, investors and end users lack a full understanding of the financial, environmental and operational benefits of energy efficiency projects which is partly due to the unavailability of long-term performance data for energy efficient appliances and equipment available in the Indian market and leads to higher risk perception. While some energy efficiency measures such as energy management systems can be implemented at no or low costs, energy efficient appliances and equipment often require higher upfront investment compared to less efficient alternatives. In a price sensitive market like India with high-risk perception of customers regarding the future performance of efficient technologies and systems, and a short-term investment perspective, this can discourage investment in solutions that deliver significant reductions in operating expenses in the long run. According to the BEE, only around 130 ESCOs are currently empanelled. While the energy efficiency market in India is estimated to be worth INR 150 000 crore, Energy Service Companies (ESCOs) only tapped about $5\%$ of this market potential (Bureau of Energy Efficiency, 2026[3]).

The Energy Savings Insurance (ESI) scheme could be instrumental in overcoming persisting market barriers and mobilising the necessary investments in energy efficiency. When integrated into the country's broader financial and policy framework, ESI can enhance investor confidence, stimulate financing from financial institutions and encourage technology providers and energy service companies (ESCOs) to scale up energy efficiency solutions. Lessons from other countries that have successfully implemented an ESI scheme or other financial risk mitigation mechanisms can further inform India's approach and support the expansion of energy efficiency investments at national level.

This Energy Savings Insurance (ESI) Implementation Roadmap aims to provide a step-by-step guidance for the design and implementation of an Energy Savings Insurance scheme in India. It shall inform and guide the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), the Ministry of Power (MOP), the Insurance and Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDA) of India, as well as a range of other key stakeholders, including not only domestic financial institutions such as banks, non-banking financial institutions and insurance companies, but also insurance associations, ESCOs, energy efficiency technology providers and vendors, industry associations, validation entities, multilateral development banks and international institutions active in India.

What is an Energy Saving Insurance (ESI) scheme?

An Energy Savings Insurance (ESI) scheme is an instrument designed to mitigate the performance risks of energy efficiency projects, thereby enhancing the creditworthiness of the investors in energy efficient technologies and processes. The ESI product covers the energy savings commitments made by the technology supplier or ESCO under an energy performance contract for a specified period of time. If the project does not achieve the pledged savings, the provider is obliged to either make necessary improvements or to compensate the client. By creating a financial liability for the technology provider tied to their performance commitment, ESI ensures accountability. If the provider fails to honour this contractual commitment, the guarantor, usually a specialised insurance agency, will financially compensate the client.

The ESI scheme is typically implemented as a package of financial and non-financial elements, including the ESI product, a standardised energy performance contract with guaranteed savings, independent technical validation and financing. These components work together to reduce perceived risks, build trust in future energy savings among involved stakeholders, and mobilise enterprises to invest in energy efficiency solutions. In detail, it comprises:
\- A standardised, simplified energy performance contract which defines the energy savings commitment and the methodology how these are measured, validated, guaranteed and insured.
\- An independent technical validation process through a credible third-party entity, which evaluates the project's savings potential, verifies the installation and acts as an arbitrator.
\- An ESI product (often a surety bond), which insures the enterprise against the technology provider/ESO failing to fulfil their energy savings obligation.
\- Existing or new financial instruments and incentives which can be linked to EE projects with an ESI.

ESI provides a performance guarantee that the contracted energy savings will be achieved through efficiency measures implemented in the project. This is based on a contractual relationship between the technology provider and their client, including performance guarantee coverage and independent technical validation. If the project obtains bank financing, a bank-borrower relationship is created that is independent of the client-provider relationship.

The ESI model has been tested and implemented in multiple countries, including in Latin America, Europe and Asia. These examples showcase its potential to mobilise investments and achieve energy savings, while also demonstrating its adaptability to the specific national context and objectives. Lessons from other countries that have successfully implemented an ESI scheme or other financial risk mitigation mechanisms can further inform India's approach and support the expansion of energy efficiency investments at the national level. The availability of robust data collection frameworks, real-time monitoring of energy savings, and enhanced collaboration between public and private stakeholders along with improved market intelligence are among the success factors for the implementation of the ESI scheme.
About this roadmap

Based on the learnings from ESI schemes in other markets, this ESI implementation roadmap provides a step-by-step guide to its introduction in India to unlock investment in energy efficiency in high priority sectors of the economy, thereby contributing to the achievement of India's sustainable development goals. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), through its Clean Energy Finance and Investment Mobilisation (CEFIM) programme, assists emerging economies in mobilising private finance and investment for clean energy, including renewable energy, energy efficiency, transmission grids, clean hydrogen and industry transformation. It provides targeted, demand-driven support to improve domestic enabling conditions, unlock blended finance and other risk mitigation instruments, and strengthen domestic financial markets in line with the needs of each partner country. The programme supports partner countries including Colombia, Egypt, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, South Africa, Thailand and Viet Nam, as well as a broader set of emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs).

In India, the OECD CEFIM programme aims to collaborate with key national stakeholders and provide recommendations to unlock and accelerate the finance and investment needed to meet the country's clean energy goals. Following close engagement between the OECD, the Government of India, the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) and other clean energy stakeholders, the Clean Energy Finance and Investment Roadmap of India (“the CEFI Roadmap”) was launched in October 2022 (OECD, 2022[8]). The CEFI Roadmap provided non-prescriptive recommendations for the Government of India to strengthen the domestic enabling environment to scale up finance and investment in (i) energy efficiency in micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), as well as (ii) offshore wind power and (iii) green hydrogen production. The CEFI Roadmap was developed in collaboration with and guided by cross-ministerial working groups and conducting multiple stakeholder consultations between 2021 and 2022, involving more than 50 national and international organisations. This process helped identify key barriers and opportunities, innovative financing solutions and investment mechanisms for unlocking investment in those three clean energy sectors. Based on the government's priorities and extensive stakeholder consultations, the establishment of an Energy Savings Insurance (ESI) scheme emerged as one of the CEFI Roadmap's key recommendations to accelerate energy efficiency improvements.

Building on the CEFI Roadmap recommendations, the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) of the Indian Ministry of Power identified the ESI scheme as a key initiative to boost energy efficiency financing, particularly for MSMEs. Consequently, the OECD CEFIM programme organised focused discussions and an international workshop on “Energy Efficiency De-Risking Instruments in India: The Role of Energy Savings Insurance and Other Instruments” in February 2024. Building on these discussions, the BEE tasked the OECD CEFIM programme with developing a needs assessment and implementation roadmap for the ESI scheme.

Developing an ESI implementation roadmap necessitates collaboration and backing from key stakeholders, such as the BEE under the Ministry of Power, the Ministry of MSMEs, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), commercial banks, insurance companies and other financial institutions, large industries, energy efficiency solution providers/ESCOs and MSMEs. The implementation of an ESI scheme further benefits from technical and financial contributions of development partners, multilateral development banks (MDBs), regional development banks and other development finance institutions (DFIs). Following its mandate, the OECD CEFIM programme, in collaboration with the BEE and supported by the International Institute for Energy Conservation (IIEC), conducted a series of consultation workshops with ESCOs, MSMEs, energy efficiency technology providers and energy auditors in October 2024.

On 20 $^{th}$ March 2025, the OECD in partnership with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) organised a joint roundtable consultation on “De-Risking Instruments for Energy Efficiency Finance in India: The role of energy savings insurance and other instruments” with financing institutions and insurance companies in Mumbai, India. The IIEC facilitated the delivery of the workshop and provided technical inputs. The suggested structure for the ESI scheme and a case for the design and implementation of an ESI pilot was presented to the stakeholders for their inputs and suggestions, which were later incorporated in this roadmap.

2 Unlocking energy efficiency investment in India

Unlocking the potential of India's energy efficiency market is critical to achieve energy affordability, economic competitiveness and poverty reduction, as well as climate goals. Over the past two decades, the country has made significant progress in expanding electricity access to over 700 million people and driving clean energy adoption, including solar power generation and energy-efficient technologies. Energy policy reforms have significantly contributed to achieving an affordable, secure and sustainable energy system, leading to remarkable growth in renewable energy capacity and energy efficiency improvement. Energy consumption per unit of GDP (energy intensity) in India has decreased over the past decade, indicating progress towards higher energy efficiency and sustainable development. The total primary energy supply per 1 000 INR of GDP declined from 0.006 toe/1 000 INRs in 2013-14 to 0.005 toe/1 000 INRs in 2023-24, suggesting enhanced energy efficiency and utilisation. Similarly, total final energy consumption per 1 000 INR of GDP decreased by $2\%$ annually between 2014 and 2024 (Bureau of Energy Efficiency, 2024[1]).

As one prominent example, the UJALA LED scheme, launched in 2015, has distributed over 368.7 million LED bulbs by January 2025 and led to the sale of 407.92 crore (4 079.2 million) LED bulbs in the Indian market, saving approximately 48 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity and reducing the retail price of LED bulbs from INR 300-350 (USD 3.80-4.50) to less than INR 80 (USD 1.0) per unit (Press Information Bureau, 2024[9]). Another example is India's Perform, Achieve, Trade (PAT) Scheme, a market-based white certificate scheme launched in 2012 to reduce specific energy consumption of energy-intensive industries such as iron and steel, cement or textiles. The market-based mechanism enhances its cost effectiveness by certifying excess energy savings, which can be traded by the respective designated consumers. By 2025, the PAT scheme covered over 1 300 designated consumers in energy intensive industries, or about $55\%$ of total industrial energy consumption, and achieved almost 26 Mtoe energy savings (Bureau of Energy Efficiency, 2026[10]). Furthermore, 9 industry sectors, including steel and refineries, are gradually transitioning into the new Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) by 2026-27, while the remaining 4 will continue under the PAT scheme (Ministry of Power, 2024[11]). In parallel, India's renewable energy capacity continues to expand, with 4.4 gigawatt (GW) capacity allocated to various RE developers in January 2025. This brings the total installed renewable power capacity to around 218 GW by February 2025 (JMK Research & Analytics, n.d.[12]). However, achieving the government's ambitious target of $50\%$ installed power capacity from non-fossil fuels and reducing emissions intensity by $45\%$ by 2030 will require a significant scale-up in energy efficiency investments.
Market opportunity - scale and limitations
Scale of opportunities

India's energy efficiency market holds immense potential, driven by rapid industrialisation, urbanisation and increasing energy demand. According to estimates by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), energy efficiency investments across key sectors could reach INR 1 002 329 to 1 320 630 crores (USD 121-160 billion) by 2031 (OECD, 2024[13]). These investments can significantly reduce energy consumption, lower operational costs and support India's climate goals, including achieving net-zero emissions by 2070.

The energy efficiency market in India holds immense scalability potential, yet according to the BEE, only around 130 ESCOs are currently empanelled which have a critical role in implementing energy efficiency measures at their clients and mobilising financing. The energy efficiency market in India is estimated to be worth INR 150 000 crore, whereas Energy Service Companies (ESCOs) only tapped about 5% of this market potential to date (Bureau of Energy Efficiency, 2026[3]). The following list summarises key areas of opportunities:

\- Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs): As of April 2026, India has over 79 million MSMEs across different economic sectors that are registered with the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. With around 16.6 million MSMEs (Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, 2026[14]), the manufacturing sector has been the source of income for 110 million employees, of which 50 million are based in rural areas (Shivprasad, 2026[15]). As per the Ministry of MSMEs, the sector consumes $25\%$ of industrial energy consumption. The energy consumption of the sector is expected to increase by $50\%$ by 2030, driven by India's economic growth, the emergence and growth of MSMEs, the impact of e-commerce and globalisation, and the ongoing transition to a low-carbon energy system. The sector is critical to align India's growth with a net-zero emissions and inclusive trajectory. Key sectors including foundry, textiles, food processing and brickmaking, currently dominate industrial energy use. More than $90\%$ of enterprises in these sectors are micro enterprises. The definition of MSMEs by size is provided in Table 2.1 below. Targeted interventions and the adoption of energy-efficient technologies can significantly reduce energy consumption while enhancing cost-effectiveness. Upgrading to energy efficient motors of IE3 and IE4 classification, for instance, can achieve $10 - 15\%$ of savings, installing variable speed drives (VSDs) for motors, and particularly for fans and pumps, can yield $10 - 15\%$ lower energy consumption during fluctuating load requirements, while the adoption of automated temperature-controlled furnaces can achieve $20 - 30\%$ savings. While SMEs are key beneficiaries for the implementation of an ESI scheme, its implementation also entails transaction costs for the insurance and validation processes. International experience shows that ESI works best for energy efficiency projects between USD 20000 and USD 1 million, whereas transaction costs might prevent its cost-effective application for micro-enterprises with investments in energy efficient systems up to USD 20000. For larger-scale investments above USD 1 million, energy performance contracts based on shared savings can offer a suitable alternative as well.

Challenges

Despite its potential, India's energy efficiency market faces several challenges that complicate the acceleration of energy efficiency improvements and scaling up of investments, particularly with a view to MSMEs. Some of the most important market barriers include:
\- Limited understanding of end-users and financial institutions of energy efficiency and other energy-related aspects.

\- Competing investment priorities of MSMEs that are more directly linked to their core business and often higher upfront investment costs of EE solutions compared to cheaper, inefficient alternatives.
\- Lack of standardised monitoring and verification processes for energy savings complicates their validation and can lead to disagreements.
\- Lack of trust of MSMEs regarding the technology provider's ability to achieve the promised energy savings.
\- Inconsistent Reporting: Energy usage data across all sectors is often fragmented, making it difficult to benchmark performance.
\- Lack of Granular Data: Detailed, sector-specific data on energy efficiency adoption is limited, making market assessments less precise.

\- The lack of a standardised mechanism for collecting, analysing and disseminating energy consumption data across various sectors makes it difficult to assess progress and identify investment priorities.

\- Limited Transparency in Financing: Information on private sector investments in energy efficiency projects, technology performance and default rates remains scarce, restricting financial institutions from accurately assessing risk and potential returns.
\- Limited Access to Finance: There is still limited access to timely and adequate formal credit for MSMEs and ESCOs.
\- Shortage of Skilled Labour, including limited availability of certified installers and auditors, as well as accredited ESCOs, which limits the uptake of energy efficiency improvement measures.

\- Market Access Constraints for smaller energy technology providers and ESCOs, due to intense competition from large companies and in export markets.

The limited awareness among MSMEs, financiers and insurers about the benefits, potentials and business model of energy efficiency is often combined with a lack of capacity to assess energy efficiency opportunities and their risks, to design and implement energy efficiency measures and monitor the savings achieved, a relatively high perception of risks, as well as limited access to financing and competing investment priorities, particularly for MSMEs.

A strong and supportive policy environment including regulatory measures, information and capacity building as well as incentives for energy efficiency improvements is critically important for the sustainable development of an energy efficiency market in India. The success of financial risk mitigation instruments such as ESI would further require the availability of robust data collection frameworks, real-time monitoring of energy savings and improved market intelligence, combined with a strong collaboration between public and private stakeholders.

3 The potential of MSMEs to become first adopters of an energy savings insurance in India

Micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) form the backbone of India's economy, driving industrialisation, employment generation and economic development. MSMEs promote inclusive growth by creating jobs in urban and rural areas, which helps to reduce regional disparities and limit rural-to-urban migration by strengthening local livelihoods. They contribute to fostering innovation in various industries, and account for about 30% of India's GDP.

The OECD conducted a needs assessment study in 2024, which identified MSMEs as high-impact sector for the implementation of an ESI scheme in India. As of April 2026, India has over 79 million MSMEs across different economic sectors that are registered with the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, creating jobs for over 350 million people. About 16.6 million or $21\%$ are active in the manufacturing sector, while services account for $36\%$ and trading for roughly $43\%$ (Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, 2026[14]). As of recent reports, the MSME contribution to GDP stands at around $30\%$ of India's total GDP and $45\%$ of manufacturing output (Bureau of Energy Efficiency, 2024[1]). Their ability to adapt and innovate has made them a driving force for job creation, skill development and regional economic balance.

As explained in Chapter 3, there are nevertheless obstacles to the contribution of MSMEs to energy efficiency improvement and to the GDP such as information asymmetries, limited access to credit and regulatory challenges. Realising India's vision of becoming a USD 5 trillion economy depends on strengthening this sector.

The BEE strives to align the ESI Scheme with the “Assistance for Deployment of Energy Efficient Technologies in Industrial Establishments (ADEETIE) Scheme” of the Ministry of Power, which was launched in 2025. ADEETIE provides support to MSMEs through fiscal financial incentives in the form of interest rate subsidies on loans to implement energy efficient technologies. The ADEETIE Scheme aims to support manufacturing enterprises operating in industrial clusters across 14 energy-intensive sectors: Brass, Bricks, Ceramic, Chemical, Fishery, Food Processing, Forging, Foundry, Glass & Refractory, Leather, Paper, Pharma, Steel Re-rolling and Textile. Based on their energy savings potential and stakeholder interest expressed during the roadmap consultations, the implementation of pilot projects in selected industrial clusters in the forging, steel re-rolling, food processing and paper sectors appear promising. At a later stage, further areas such as public or commercial buildings could be explored for the application of the ESI scheme.

MSMEs operate in two major industrial sectors, namely manufacturing and service industries, engaging in activities ranging from textile production, food processing and engineering goods to IT services, retail and logistics. The Government's procurement policy aims to promote MSME growth by reserving a certain percentage of contracts for MSMEs (Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, 2012[18]).

Preparatory phase
Stakeholder engagement and consultations

As part of the preparatory efforts to introduce an ESI scheme in India, the support from key stakeholders needs to be mobilised to ensure a sustainable anchoring in the Indian market and sufficient uptake of the insurance product. Key domestic stakeholders for the ESI scheme include the General Insurance Council (GIC), participating banks under the ADEETIE scheme and other interested financial market institutions, insurance companies (to be identified with support from GIC), the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDAI), ESCOs and energy efficiency technology providers. The implementation of an ESI scheme further benefits from technical and financial contributions of development partners, multilateral development banks (MDBs), regional development banks and other development finance institutions (DFIs).

Preparatory work to mobilise stakeholder support has commenced through a series of stakeholder consultations conducted between 2024 and 2025. The General Insurance Council (GIC) was constituted in 2001 by the IRDAI under section 64-C of the Insurance Act, 1938. The GIC is an important link between the IRDAI and the non-life insurance industry, and it advocates the industry's interests with the government, and is mandated to facilitate overall growth of the insurance industry in a fair and equitable manner in the interest of all stakeholders. The Council also works with the International Insurance Associations and agencies for information exchange and for the promotion of business collaborations. During the stakeholder workshop in March 2025, the GIC expressed their support in working with the OECD, the BEE and the ADB to support the design and implementation of the ESI scheme. The GIC's role as association of insurance companies in India would be to encourage its members to explore the energy efficiency market as a potential business opportunity, and to develop and file an ESI product for registration.

During the roundtable meeting organised on 20 $^{th}$ March 2025 in Mumbai, the IRDAI confirmed its support in approving an ESI product once it is filed by the insurance companies in India and compliant with all applicable regulations.

Most of the leading banks in India, especially the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI), ICICI Bank, HSBC Bank, YES Bank, HDFC Bank and the State Bank of India have experience in financing energy savings projects and understand the energy efficiency market. Several banks including HDFC and ICICI already have insurance vehicles (HDFC-ERGO, ICICI Lombard, etc.) and have commitments for financing MSMEs under the ADEETIE Scheme. The BEE could work with these banks to encourage them to (i) provide the guarantee for the performance and the payment, or (ii) work through their insurance verticals to develop and file an ESI product, for instance a surety bond, for approval from IRDAI. If a guarantee is preferred, insurance providers can offer a financial guarantee through the ESCO for fulfilling its obligation as per the agreed terms. If an ESI product in the form of a surety bond is preferred, the GIC could support in expediting the process.
ESI implementation plan in India

As large domestic banks already have experience with energy efficiency projects, the development of dedicated ESI products through their insurance verticals appears as a promising approach. Surety bonds have been used in many instances for the implementation of ESI schemes, for instance in Colombia and in Europe. The HDFC-ERGO Insurance Company, a vertical of HDFC Bank, is already in discussion with Munich Re for a possible launch of an energy efficiency insurance product. To date, the insurance sector in India has, however, not insured any energy efficiency project.
Needs assessment and priority sectors

A detailed needs assessment aims to gather information on the existing policy and regulatory framework to support the financing and implementation of energy efficiency projects, to assess the readiness of the insurance sector and identify a suitable host agency for the implementation of ESI scheme. The needs assessment also helps in identifying high impact sectors, assessing the energy efficiency financing landscape and identifying potential clients that would benefit most from the implementation of the ESI scheme.

The OECD CEFIM programme, under the guidance of the BEE, conducted a needs assessment study for an ESI scheme in 2024, which identified the MSME sector, particularly the manufacturing industry, as a priority sector for the initial rollout of the scheme. While different industrial sub-sectors dominate in each of India's states and Union Territories, foundry and forging, textiles, food processing and brickmaking are most frequently represented in the roughly 180 MSME clusters across India. Consultation meetings and workshops were conducted between 2022 and 2025 to engage with key stakeholders including financial institutions, insurance companies, ESCOs, MSMEs, technology providers, vendors and international agencies working in India.

During the needs assessment and industry consultation phase, insurance service providers have shown interest in insuring energy saving projects in India. During the consultation phase, Indian stakeholders suggested introducing a hybrid financial de-risking instrument comprising of (i) a credit guarantee provided by an international financial institution supporting the energy efficiency project financing and (ii) an ESI product backing up the agreed energy savings.

Both the ESI scheme and the ADEETIE scheme focus on accelerating energy efficiency improvements in MSMEs in the industry sector. Linking both schemes could enhance their impact, where the participating financial institutions under the ADEETIE scheme finance energy efficiency technologies and measures in SMEs, where an ESI can be included as a performance guarantee mechanism for the project. Box 4.1. Assistance for the Deployment of Energy Efficient Technologies in Industrial Establishments (ADEETIE) scheme

The Ministry of Power has launched the ADEETIE scheme to accelerate the uptake of energy efficient technologies and measures by MSMEs through financial instruments and provide technical assistance in carrying out investment grade energy audits, in preparing detailed project reports, in monitoring and verification of the implementation, and in promotion and awareness raising activities. The scheme provides a 5% (to small and micro enterprises) and 3% (to medium enterprises) interest subsidy on loans from participating financial institutions for technology adoption.

The scheme is designed to help manufacturing businesses in India become more energy efficient. Enterprises operating in MSME clusters across the following energy-intensive sectors are eligible for support: 1. Brass, 2. Bricks, 3. Ceramic, 4. Chemical, 5. Fishery, 6. Food Processing, 7. Forging, 8. Foundry, 9. Glass & Refractory, 10. Leather, 11. Paper, 12, Pharma, 13. Steel Re-rolling, and 14. Textile.

The scheme will be implemented in a phased manner, initially focusing on 60 clusters. In the first three-year phase (FY 2024-25 to FY 2026-27), up to 9 000 MSME units may be covered, followed by another 100 clusters in the second phase. This phased approach allows for demonstrating success and streamlining the scheme based on learnings from the initial phase.

A market feasibility study on “Financial De-Risking Instruments for Energy Efficiency in India”, conducted by the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in April 2025, recommended the design and implementation of a pilot project for an ESI scheme in the MSME sector. The BEE and the OECD CEFIM programme would work with the ADB and other key stakeholders to support the design and implementation of a pilot.
Identification of pilot clusters

For a pilot implementation of an ESI scheme, MSME clusters have to be determined. The needs assessment study revealed that while different industrial sub-sectors dominate in each of India's states and Union Territories, foundry and forging, textiles, food processing and brickmaking are most frequently represented in the roughly 180 MSME clusters across India. In consultations with the Bureau of Energy Efficiency, the foundry and paper manufacturing clusters near Coimbatore district in Tamil Nadu and the forging cluster near New Delhi emerged as potential pilot clusters. Both clusters are part of the ADEETIE scheme, have significant energy savings potential and indicated their readiness to participate in the design and implementation of ESI pilot projects. Pilot implementation of the ESI scheme will likely require the mobilisation of additional capital, for instance through multilateral development banks and development partners. The specific design of the pilot projects would be determined by the BEE as facilitator, with technical support from the OECD CEFIM programme and selected ESCOs, and with financial support from domestic and potentially international financial institutions.
Design of the ESI structure

As a next step, the ESI implementation structure needs to be defined and key stakeholders and their responsibilities identified. The proposed ESI implementation structure for India covers financial and non-financial components to mitigate project risks and create investor (bank) and client (ESCOs on behalf of MSMEs) confidence. The structure explains the roles of the ESI Service Providers, financial institutions, ESCOs, independent validation entity, MSMEs and the mechanism for fund flow.

The ESCO aggregates and designs the energy efficiency project at the cluster level for the participating MSMEs. This aggregation shall ensure the needed scale for financing and insuring energy savings by the banks and insurance companies respectively but also helps to ensure profitability for ESCOs.

A standardised contract signed between the MSME cluster and the ESCO will guarantee the project's performance in terms of energy savings or power generation and is backed by an energy savings insurance product that is activated in case of underperformance. The MSMEs are typically the beneficiaries of the energy savings insurance. Project validation is carried out by an independent validating entity with experience in certification of energy projects, which also acts as an arbitrator with binding decisions for all parties to the contract. Financing may be provided by participating financial institutions interested in creating an energy efficiency lending portfolio. This may include participating banks under the ADEETIE scheme. Empanelled banks under the ADEETIE scheme or more broadly participating financial institutions could receive additional support through (i) government financing under the ADEETIE scheme, or (ii) credit guarantees provided by an international financial institution/MDB. text: Under the proposed ESI structure, the participating banks can activate the ESI by establishing insurance coverage as a credit requirement. The ESI reduces the risk of non-payment of the credit, since it guarantees the promised savings. In case the guaranteed savings are not achieved and the ESCO is not able to cover the shortfall, the ESI financially compensates the entity which invested in the energy efficiency project for the shortfall in insured savings.

These include public and private sector agencies, financial institutions, validation entities, ESCOs, individual experts and energy auditors, IT and communications experts, regulatory bodies and international institutions.

Implementation Phase
Facilitating entity

Based on a thorough market and needs assessment and further preparatory work, the design of the ESI scheme needs to be aligned with existing policies and regulations, and complementary to existing programmes and initiatives. A significant amount of technical assistance and capacity building for banks and insurance companies, but also ESCOs and technology providers is typically required. Determining a single facilitating entity is beneficial to co-ordinate involved stakeholders, guide the process and provide technical assistance for vetting the key parameters at different stages of design and implementation. Either the OECD, with support from key international and local institutions, or a dedicated Indian institution could facilitate the rollout of the ESI scheme in India.
Proposed timeline - 1 Month after the ESI Roadmap launch
Independent validation entity and definition of monitoring and verification methodologies

Project validation plays a vital role in ensuring credibility and accuracy of energy savings calculations for energy efficiency projects. Under the ESI model, an independent third-party review validates that measurement reports comply with established guidelines and reflect actual performance. This process enhances transparency and trust by objectively assessing the reported savings based on an agreed methodology and confirming that calculations are based on a well-defined baseline and relevant operational factors.

The BEE could select a recognised and trusted validation entity, assigning it a mandate to establish a credible energy consumption baseline before project implementation and to conduct the validation in the case of a claim filed by the ESCO or MSME for not achieving the agreed energy savings. In case energy efficiency is a new area of work for such validation entity, (i) training and capacity building for their validation team members might be required, and/or (ii) the validation entity might opt to hire BEE-certified energy auditors and managers as validators. The validation entity would be in charge of defining the monitoring and verification methodologies for the technical validation of energy savings, as well as all the mechanisms, templates and forms that guide the implementation of the scheme. Common validation methodologies are derived from internationally recognised procedures, such as the IPMVP or ISO.
Proposed timeline - Months 1-3
ENERGY SAVINGS INSURANCE IMPLEMENTATION ROADMAP OF INDIA © OECD 2026
Standardised energy performance contract

The BEE could work with ESCOs, financial institutions, GIC and the development partners, regional and multilateral development banks and other development finance institutions and international organisations providing technical assistance (e.g. the OECD and ADB) to develop a standardised and simplified energy performance contract. This standardised energy performance contract should be developed and vetted by a law firm experienced in the field of energy, mortgage and insurance to ensure compliance with domestic regulations and legal practices. The contract should reflect the roles and responsibilities of the parties to the agreement, the terms for the technology selection and supply, installation and maintenance. The standardised contract should further include an energy savings guarantee and clearly define the roles of the insurance product and the independent validation entity.

The contract should establish the responsibilities of the technology provider regarding the supply and installation of equipment and clearly define the agreed performance guarantee in terms of promised savings or energy generation. On the client's (MSMEs) side, the contract determines the terms for timely payment, the provision of access to the facilities and appropriate equipment maintenance. Among the most significant features of the contract are:
\- Contract duration
\- Savings guarantee
• Reference energy tariffs
• Periodicity of measurements
• The monitoring, verification and validation methodology
• The insurance activation criteria
\- The indemnification mechanisms for unrealised savings, and
\- Dispute resolution
Proposed timeline - Months 2-4
Energy savings insurance product

The successful implementation of the ESI model will rely on the interest and commitment of insurance companies and financial institutions to adopt an energy savings insurance product and finance energy efficiency products on condition of the adoption of such an insurance. The insurance is meant to strengthen the confidence of ESCOs, technology providers and MSMEs in the achievement of the contractually agreed energy savings commitments. The ESI contract between the ESCO and the insurance company aims to mitigate financing risks and strengthen the confidence of commercial banks and other financial institutions in providing the loans. Here, the ESI could play an important role in eliminating the requirements of many banks for collateral when providing the bank loans. The BEE could work with the GIC and its members to ensure that the ESI product is designed and filed for approval with IRDAI. Based on experience from ESI implementation in other markets, surety bonds or bank guarantees are suitable options for an energy savings insurance product, while most ESI products rely on surety bonds. Furthermore, requirements and procedures for linking the ESI with financial incentives provided under the ADEETIE scheme needs to be defined.
Proposed timeline - Months 2-4
ENERGY SAVINGS INSURANCE IMPLEMENTATION ROADMAP OF INDIA © OECD 2026
Capacity building and awareness raising campaign

The successful adoption of the ESI scheme will require training and capacity building of the key stakeholders and experts involved in its rollout in India. The BEE could work with the OECD, ADB and other international organisations, bilateral development partners, regional and multilateral development banks and other DFIs to design effective training programmes and awareness raising campaigns. These should aim to strengthen the skills of financial institutions and insurance providers in underwriting energy efficiency projects, and of ESCOs in developing and implementing effective energy efficiency measures and technologies, but also to inform the key stakeholders about the functioning of the scheme and to create momentum for its uptake. Multiple channels should be leveraged to engage key stakeholders including ESCOs, energy auditors, technology providers, commercial banks and other financial institutions, the independent validation entity, insurance and reinsurance service providers, MSMEs, Public Sector Undertakings (PSU) and the state agencies. A series of workshops, roundtables, webinars, TV and radio advertisements and other digital tools could be used to raise awareness about energy efficiency and the ESI model, while dedicated training programmes could serve to strengthen capacities.
Proposed timeline - Constant process starting from Roadmap launch and continuing for 12 months
Pilot project design

Correctly designing and implementing at least two pilot projects are key for rolling out the ESI scheme in India. This component is the combined outcome of all other components and should be designed in parallel to other ESI components. Based on the BEE's prioritisation of sectors and industrial clusters, two pilot projects in two industrial clusters in India will be developed in detail. During the pilot phase, the BEE, with support from the facilitator and financier would guide the key stakeholders on the different stages of implementing the ESI scheme. This will ensure a seamless and straightforward application of the scheme in the pilot projects. A multilateral or regional development bank like the ADB could be brought in to fund the preparatory work and pilot implementation of the ESI scheme in the selected clusters. This would include the drafting and adaptation of standardised energy performance contracts and other documents, establishing the baseline energy consumption and equipment usage, co-ordinating with banks, insurance companies, ESCOs, technology providers and other stakeholders, conducting the verification and validation of the first pilot projects. After the signing of energy performance and ESI contracts, and after obtaining a loan where needed, pilot implementation would start. While pilot projects aim to attract a high level of visibility at national and international level, the outcomes and lessons learned would help in integrating the ESI scheme with the pipeline of projects under the ADEETIE scheme.
Proposed timeline - Months 2-6
Regular monitoring and verification

Besides ensuring appropriate operation and maintenance procedures for the installed equipment, a regular monitoring and verification of the achieved savings helps to mitigate risks of defaults and shortcomings in savings. Any shortfall in savings during the pilot testing and during the initial years of implementation may lead to the loss of confidence of key stakeholders. If a savings shortfall during the initial years is correctly identified by the MSMEs/ESCOs and confirmed by the validation entity, the provider should either take technical correction measures or compensate the client (MSME). Should the provider fail to compensate the client, the insurance would be triggered to financially compensate the beneficiary according to the contract terms. Thereby, the insurance backing should ensure continued trust in the model despite a confirmed shortfall in achieved savings. The definition of appropriate and detailed monitoring, reporting and verification standards and processes is therefore of utmost importance.

The validation entity, in close co-ordination with the technology provider and the insurance company, should monitor the actual accrued energy savings on an annual basis and utilising the agreed methodology. This should avoid any requirements for a premature economic compensation due to underperformance of the technologies.

Technology providers should rely on the monitoring methodology and process agreed in the standard energy performance contract. Smart data loggers or meters can serve to collect information about the real-life use of the equipment and achieved savings.

In order to validate the achieved savings compared to the committed savings and for maintaining proper records, the following documents should be submitted by the technology provider and the ESCO to the validation entity and the insurance provider:

\- Data and photo of the data-logger (including date and time of the data collection) against the parameters as defined in the energy performance contract for each equipment type for each year of the contract. This process should be repeated on the same date every year to ensure consistency.
\- Calibration certificate of the equipment and the data-loggers or independent verification report to ensure their accuracy.

This process should be part of the validation methodology and should be performed in close consultation with the validation entity. The standard contract should clearly and in detail define the methodologies for measurement and verification. An online data management system or platform could help in recording and streamlining relevant data.

Annual monitoring and verification of energy savings using the agreed methodology should be ensured, as well as a final project evaluation and validation at the end of the energy performance contract. This will help in determining the overall savings achieved, as well as the payback period of the investment and recording of any profits after the completion of the ESI and ESCO performance contracts.
Proposed timeline - validation of project design before start of implementation, validation of installation and annual M&V of savings; final project evaluation and validation
Learning framework

Regularly document the implemented energy efficiency measures and achieved savings, as well as the lessons learned from project implementation across different sub-sectors. Based on this data, develop case studies to disseminate learnings with national and international stakeholders and mobilise the further uptake of ESI products in India.
Proposed timeline - Starting from implementation and at regular intervals
ESI rollout

Based on the learnings from the pilot projects, the BEE with technical support from the facilitator, could develop a long-term strategy to incorporate the ESI scheme fully into phase II of the ADEETIE scheme, to support financial institutions and insurance companies in developing a project pipeline for energy efficiency projects and rolling out the ESI scheme across India. The ESI model also has significant potential for implementation in the public sector, particularly as a key element in green procurement processes. Public sector actors in India are often familiar with using instruments like surety bonds and performance contract surety bonds to cover financing risks, although these have not been linked to energy savings performance in the past. The standardised contracts and independent validation create transparency and predictability of energy savings expectations and build accountability into public procurement processes. Therefore, integrating the ESI into public sector financing frameworks could be considered at a later stage to support enhancing energy efficiency in the public sector. The potential to roll out the ESI scheme to further sectors could be explored as well.

5 Facilitating the ESI implementation
Establishment of the energy consumption baseline

Reliably determining the baseline energy consumption is the first step to pursue energy efficiency or sustainability goals in a targeted manner. A good baseline doesn't just help with tracking energy savings; if the data is trustworthy and accessible, it can further help in identifying areas for improvement and in securing bank loans. Four fundamental steps are required to establish the energy consumption baseline:

\- Define the Metrics - The ESCO and validation entity are required to define metrics to collect the energy baseline data effectively. Metrics will help in comparing the baseline with future energy consumption over a period of time.
\- Normalise the Data - The next step is to normalise the baseline data to create a trustworthy comparison between the current and future years.
\- Set up Real-time Monitoring - It is the real-time data that allows facilities to be proactive in driving down energy intensity and costs.
\- Sub-meter Specific Processes - For medium to large MSMEs, it is important to capture the data at sub-meter level to ensure accuracy.

Normalisation of energy use data

A normalisation process is required for putting the data into context and enabling valid comparisons. For example - in MSME operations, it is critically important to understand energy consumption in relation to production. Measuring production-normalised energy intensity allows businesses to understand the true meaning of their energy consumption. A proper project scoping exercise should attempt to determine which factors have the biggest impact on energy consumption. In many industrial environments, production is the most important normalisation factor, while weather conditions, for instance expressed in cooling degree days, have an impact on the electricity use for space cooling. Table 5.2 below provides the required normalisation approaches. ESCOs should use them for accurate calculation of energy savings.

ApproachDescription
Multi-year averagingAveraging multiple years' data to create a more reliable baseline of energy consumption.
Production normalisationDividing energy usage by a unit of throughput to determine the energy intensity of production.
Weather normalisationDividing energy usage by a unit that quantifies the effects of weather, e.g. Cooling Degree Days.
Space normalisationDividing energy usage by the area of a facility (e.g. ft^2).
Volume normalisationDividing energy usage by the volume of a facility (e.g. ft^3). Commonly used in temperature-controlled facilities.

text: Real time monitoring

The most frequently used method for setting up the baseline is to simply tally up the utility bills to get a snapshot of monthly or annual energy spend. This approach is simple and inexpensive, but the data collected through this method isn't actionable. It does establish a baseline, but it doesn't indicate:
\- When energy usage is highest
\- When rates and demand charges are highest
\- Which systems or equipment have the highest energy consumption

In most states of India, the commercial and industrial customers don't get charged a flat rate for electricity. Most are on some form of time-of-use rate, whereby rates vary by time of the day, week and/or year. Depending on the contract, these rates may be known well in advance. It can be very helpful during the energy baseline process to understand when rates are spiking, or penalties are being applied. It may make sense to schedule maintenance during these times or even shut down the operations entirely.

Through setting up a real-time data collection system, facilities get a much clearer picture of their own patterns of energy use during working hours versus off-shift usage. This helps flag areas for improvement.

Large spikes in consumption can point the way to targeted improvements, whereas high usage across the board may point to a more capital-intensive strategy.

The utility meters with Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) data are not always a good substitute for real-time monitoring systems. AMI systems or “smart meters” are typically installed by utilities to make meter reading easier, but it is still insufficient for effective energy management, primarily because of the time lag in receiving data. Thus, real time monitoring data helps in developing a strong baseline.
Sub-metering of specific areas for more accurate data

Typically, power usage data is collected at the main meter, which does not provide enough detail for industrial operations and does not take into account potential billing errors. An energy auditor would want to double check and uncover power factors and overvoltage issues that can cost money and damage equipment. It is useful to install sub-meters to monitor the most energy-intensive processes within a facility.

Baselining specific systems in addition to whole facilities allows for a much more targeted energy management approach. While deciding on the installation of sub-meters, the boundaries should be drawn around processes rather than equipment. Sub-metering should account for all major components involved in the process and should feed into one or more of the metrics defined for the production-normalised energy intensity.

Validation process and requirements

Project validation plays a vital role in ensuring credibility and accuracy of energy savings calculations for projects using energy-efficient equipment. It involves an independent third-party review to verify that measurement reports comply with established guidelines and reflect actual performance. This process enhances transparency and trust by objectively assessing the reported savings and confirming that calculations are based on a well-defined baseline and relevant operational factors. By aligning with the principles of the ESI scheme, validation ensures consistency, reliability and compliance throughout the project lifecycle. Under the standardised contract, a two-stage validation process should be required, including: A. project validation and B. Arbitration process.
A. Project validation
\- Project validation at contractual stage.
\- Installation validation, to be conducted when the project equipment is installed and at the end of commissioning stage to check that everything is working correctly and according to the contract.

\- Annual validation during the insured period: at the end of each year, the provider reports on the savings achieved. The validation entity could be asked to review these reports. In cases of underperformance or disagreement between the parties, a review must be requested; in such cases, however, the arbitration process would already have been initiated.
B. Arbitration process
\- It can be started in cases of underperformance or disagreement between the parties on the annual savings report issued by the technology provider.

\- The validation process begins when a technology provider identifies a project opportunity or a client is seeking to upgrade to more energy-efficient equipment. As outlined above, the validation is required at three key stages during the contracting period (Figure 5.1):

The BEE certified Energy Auditors and Managers can also qualify for the validators' job as they carry the necessary knowledge. Their qualifications include:

II. Validation of project design
The project design validation focuses on verifying the estimated energy savings calculated by the technology provider based on the specific project conditions and boundaries.

To determine the estimated energy savings, the energy consumption of the existing equipment is measured and compared to the projected consumption of the new, validated equipment. This comparison accounts for key operational factors such as usage hours and other relevant parameters. As part of this validation step, project operation factors are established to enable an accurate assessment of energy savings after one year. Project operation factors are typically set in the validation methodologies and agreed between the provider and the client. They serve as an input for the validation entity. Once the committed energy savings value is validated, clearance is given for the activation of the ESI contract. This contract will include all relevant operational factors and the verified committed energy savings. The energy savings calculation methodology for the annual verification of energy savings and any potential insurance claim needs to be agreed. III. Verification and validation of project implementation

The project implementation or installation validation involves a site visit conducted by the validator to verify that the correct equipment has been installed as per the project documentation and the equipment is fully operational. During this visit, the validator performs a visual inspection to confirm proper installation and functionality of the system. Additionally, the validator examines the mandatory data logger, which is installed by the technology provider to facilitate the recording of key operational parameters as defined in the design stage. Upon completion of the site visit, the validator issues an installation validation report, documenting the implementation status and ensuring compliance with project requirements. This report verifies that the technology and data logger have been correctly installed in accordance with project requirements. The following documents are required for implementation validation:
• Final project documentation
\- As outlined in the ESI contract, each equipment type should adhere to the initial design scope.
\- Manufacturer's datasheet of installed data logger
\- Provides technical specifications to confirm the eligibility of the data logger.
\- Valid calibration certificate or independent verification report
\- Confirmation that the data logger meets ESI methodology requirements and proper calibration.
\- The data logger calibration must be valid for the upcoming annual measurement period.
These documents collectively ensure that the implementation/installation meets ESI standards, allowing for accurate performance monitoring and savings validation.
IV. Annual validation of the project

After the end of each year, the provider reports on the energy savings achieved to support the annual validation of the savings. This is based on the same operating factors outlined in the ESI contract. This process determines whether economic compensation is necessary due to underperformance of the installed technology. To facilitate this process, the client (MSME/ESCO) and the technology provider must agree on the following factors during the design stage:
• The defined units of transformed energy
• The predetermined cost per energy unit
\- The committed energy savings value, calculated as per the agreed ESI methodology
This structured approach ensures that actual savings align with initial projections, providing a clear basis for performance evaluation.
